chunks.page_content: The remnant of the county of Auvergne resulted from the usurpation of William VII "the Young" of Auvergne around 1155 by his uncle William VIII the Old. Some authors have named William VII "the Young" of Auvergne and his descendants "counts of Clermont". William VII "the Young" of Auvergne was a Count of the region of Auvergne, France. Still others choose to call the successors of William VII "the Young" of Auvergne the "counts-dauphins of Auvergne" out of convenience. The dauphinate of Auvergne was in reality the remnant of the county of Auvergne. William VIII the Old was the uncle of William VII "the Young" of Auvergne. The majority of authors choose to call William VII "the Young" of Auvergne and his successors the dauphins of Auvergne. William VII "the Young" of Auvergne's mother was the daughter of the Dauphin de Viennois Guigues IV. William VII "the Young" of Auvergne was the first Count of Auvergne to be given the title Dauphin (Prince). William VII "the Young" of Auvergne was able to maintain his status in part of his county. William VII "the Young" of Auvergne accompanied the French king Louis VII on the Second Crusade. Naming William VII "the Young" of Auvergne and his descendants "counts of Clermont" risks confusion with the county of Clermont in Beauvaisais. William VII "the Young" of Auvergne's male descendants were usually given "Dauphin" as a second name. Naming William VII "the Young" of Auvergne and his descendants "counts of Clermont" risks confusion with the episcopal county of Clermont in Auvergne. William VII "the Young" of Auvergne maintained his status especially in Beaumont, Chamalières, and Montferrand. The title of dauphin of Auvergne was derived from William VII "the Young" of Auvergne's mother. William VII "the Young" of Auvergne was Count of the region of Auvergne, France during the years 1145–1168.
